title: Profitable groceries, unprofitable warehouses
lede: Webvan’s problem was not the price of a box of cereal. Its gross margin was healthy by grocery standards. What it couldn’t cover was the fixed cost of the machine built to deliver that cereal.

blocks.source: Derived from the 2000 10-K[^3]: G&A of $292.3M, a 26.5% gross margin and the $104 average order. The order estimate is $178.5M of sales ÷ $104 ÷ 365. These are our calculations, not company figures.

blocks.title: What one day of overhead cost, counted in grocery orders

left.label: of general and administrative cost for every day of 2000 (derived)[^3]

unit.label: batches of 100 orders, each order leaving $27.56 of gross profit after paying for the groceries (derived)

blocks.equation: $292.3M of G&A ÷ 365 days = $801K a day. $104 average order × 26.5% gross margin = $27.56. $801K ÷ $27.56 ≈ 29,057 orders a day, drawn as 291 carts of 100 orders each. Our estimate of actual volume in 2000 is about 4,700 orders a day, or 47 of these carts. All inputs are from the 10-K[^3]; Webvan did not disclose order counts.
blocks.source: Derived from three inputs in the 2000 10-K[^3]: $292.3M of G&A, a 26.5% gross margin and a $104 average order. These are our calculations, not company figures.
